narrative:
The model predicted that you have a 59% chance of failing the bar exam on your first attempt. Because this probability is above 50%, the admissions system automatically rejected your law school application.

Your rejection was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. The strongest influence came from your third-year grades, which placed you in the second decile of your class. This was substantially weaker than the average of nearly sixth-decile performance among students who were accepted, and it pushed the prediction strongly toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 3.60 was the second most important factor; because it is noticeably higher than the 3.23 average of accepted students, it worked in your favor and pulled the prediction back toward passing. Your LSAT score of 27 was the third most influential piece of information. This score is well below the 37-point average of accepted applicants and therefore pushed the outcome back toward likely failure.

Taken together, the model saw your lower class-rank performance and modest LSAT result as outweighing the positive signal from your strong college GPA, resulting in an overall outlook of probable bar exam failure.

You should focus on improving your LSAT score and, if possible, strengthening your academic record before reapplying. Consider targeted test-preparation courses, practice exams, or even a post-baccalaureate program that could demonstrate upward academic momentum. These steps would directly address the factors that most hurt your current prediction. (218 words)
